introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2021. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
enonce_intro_markdown: **SECTION D: WORLD, 1919 TO THE PRESENT DATE**
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections ». `regles_choix` porte une règle « 1 sur 3 » par section (A, B, C, D), ce qui correspond exactement à la consigne imprimée ; la consigne complète est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : chaque question porte 25 marks imprimés (« All questions carry equal marks »), soit 100 points pour les quatre questions à traiter. Aucun écart de points constaté ; `points` vaut 25 pour l'exercice et pour l'unique question de chaque fichier.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde et questions 1 à 12) ; publicités, filigranes gcerevision.com et mention manuscrite d'adresse web ignorés ; aucune question coupée ni illisible, aucune figure ni carte dans le sujet.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées au niveau Advanced Level (introduction, développement, conclusion argumentée). Aucune statistique ni citation n'est avancée ; les effectifs sont donnés en ordres de grandeur prudents (« roughly nine to ten million », « about two million »).

Question 2 : l'énoncé imprimé associe « the Jihad in Futa Jallon » aux dates 1854-1864. Ces dates correspondent à la guerre sainte d'Al-Hajj Umar Tall (empire toucouleur, parti de Dinguiraye, en bordure du Fouta-Djalon), alors que le jihad du Fouta-Djalon proprement dit date d'environ 1725 (Karamoko Alfa). Le sujet est recopié tel quel ; le corrigé signale la divergence et traite le mouvement de 1854-1864, avec le jihad du Fouta-Djalon en arrière-plan. L'année de début de la guerre sainte d'Umar est donnée de façon prudente (1852 ou 1854 selon les sources).

Question 2 : détails à vérifier par un historien (siège de Médine en 1857, prise de Ségou en 1861 et de Hamdallahi en 1862, mort d'Umar en 1864, chute de Ségou face à Archinard en 1890) ; ils sont cités conformément à l'historiographie courante, mais le corrigé ne s'appuie pas sur des chiffres.

Question 7 : les dates de 1688 sont données en style ancien (naissance du prince le 10 juin, invitation des « Immortal Seven » et acquittement des sept évêques le 30 juin, débarquement à Torbay le 5 novembre) ; le corrigé précise le choix du calendrier julien.
Question 4 : le massacre de Thiaroye (décembre 1944), les émeutes d'Accra (1948) et la conférence de Brazzaville (1944) sont cités sans bilan chiffré, le nombre exact de victimes étant discuté.

Question 5 : exemples de coups d'État (Togo 1963, Ghana 1966, Nigeria 1966, Ouganda 1971, Éthiopie 1974, Mali 2020) cités sans chiffres ; la formule « very many people were killed » remplace volontairement tout bilan sous Amin, très discuté.

Question 12 : la liste des suspensions et départs (Nigeria 1995, Fidji, Zimbabwe 2003, Gambie 2013 puis retour 2018) et l'adhésion du Cameroun en 1995 sont citées de mémoire historique ; aucun chiffre financier n'est avancé.

Questions à thème régional : les noms de thèmes sont qualifiés (par exemple `military coups in africa`, `refugee crisis in africa`, `league of nations`) pour éviter les collisions avec les Tags de l'Histoire francophone ; à reverifier à l'ingestion avec `find_tag_variant`.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Why was the Cold War inevitable after the Second World War?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The Cold War was the period of hostility without direct large-scale fighting between the United States and its allies and the Soviet Union and its allies, from about 1945-47 until 1989-91. It was fought through ideology, propaganda, an arms race, alliances, economic aid and proxy conflicts. The question asks why it was inevitable. The best answer explains the structural and ideological factors that made rivalry very probable, while noting that some historians consider that the form it took depended on choices that were not inevitable.

**1. Reasons why it was inevitable.**
- *Ideological incompatibility.* The United States stood for capitalism, liberal democracy and free markets; the Soviet Union for Marxism-Leninism, a one-party state and a planned economy. Each side believed that the other's system threatened its own, and the ideological hostility dated back to the Russian Revolution of 1917 and the Western intervention in the Russian Civil War.
- *The wartime alliance was one of necessity.* The Grand Alliance against Hitler was an alliance of convenience. Mistrust remained: the Soviets resented the delay in opening a second front in Western Europe until 1944 and Western secrecy about the atomic bomb, while the West resented the Nazi-Soviet Pact of 1939.
- *The power vacuum in Europe.* Germany was defeated and Europe was exhausted, leaving the United States and the Soviet Union as the only superpowers. Their armies met in the centre of Europe, and each tried to make its position secure.
- *Disagreements over Germany and Eastern Europe.* At Yalta (February 1945) the Allies agreed on free elections in Eastern Europe, but the Red Army occupied the region and Stalin installed communist-controlled governments, regarding them as a security buffer. The United States and Britain saw this as expansion. At Potsdam (July-August 1945) there were disagreements over reparations and the future of Germany, and the new US President Truman was less willing to accommodate Stalin than Roosevelt had been.
- *Atomic weapons.* The US use of atomic bombs on Japan in August 1945 and its monopoly made the Soviet Union feel threatened, and it developed its own bomb in 1949, which started an arms race.
- *Mutual fear and policies of containment.* Kennan's "Long Telegram" (1946) and Churchill's "Iron Curtain" speech at Fulton (March 1946) shaped Western policy; the Truman Doctrine (March 1947) and the Marshall Plan (June 1947) committed the United States to contain communism, and the Soviet Union replied with the Cominform (1947) and the consolidation of its bloc. The currency reform in Germany and the Berlin Blockade (1948-49) led to the formation of NATO (1949), and later to the Warsaw Pact (1955).

**2. Limits to the argument of inevitability.**
- Some historians (the revisionists and post-revisionists) argue that misunderstanding, personalities and decisions mattered: Stalin's caution in some cases, Truman's tough approach after Roosevelt's death, and the contribution of American economic expansion. A different series of decisions might have produced a less intense rivalry.
- Cooperation was possible in the early United Nations and in some of the peace treaties. Yet the basic structure (two superpowers with opposing ideologies and security interests) made some conflict probable.

**Conclusion.** The Cold War was virtually inevitable because of ideological hostility, mutual mistrust, the end of the common enemy, the power vacuum in Europe and disagreements over Germany and Eastern Europe, reinforced by the atomic bomb. Only its precise form and timing (for example the Berlin Blockade, the Korean War and the arms race) depended on decisions and events.
